lesson.grammar_point: modals of deduction in the present and in the past

listenings.text: The students who read the most are often the slowest on the reading section, and I think I know why. They were trained to find the answer in the text. They see a question, go back to the passage, and look for the sentence that says it. On an inference question, that sentence does not exist. The text gives you two facts, and the answer is what must be true if both facts are true. So here is the exercise I give everyone. Before you look at the options, answer the question in your own words. If your answer is something the text could not possibly support, you are guessing. If it follows from two sentences, you have made an inference. Then look at the options, and choose the one that says your answer in different words.

Good morning, everyone. A few changes at the law library this week. Because of the exam period, the second floor is now reserved for silent study, and phones must be switched off before you go up the stairs. The group rooms on the first floor are in high demand, so they can only be booked online, for a maximum of two hours. If you booked a room last week by email, please book it again on the website, because those requests were not saved. On Friday the library closes at six instead of ten, for maintenance. And finally, the printer on the ground floor is not working. The one on the first floor is.

reading.rtitle: The Answer Is Not on the Page
paras: Students who read well in their own language often struggle with the TOEFL reading section, and the reason is rarely vocabulary. They read every word, look for the sentence that contains the answer, and lose time when that sentence is not there. In most questions it is not there, because the test is not checking whether you can find words. It is checking whether you can understand what the words mean together.

Since January 2026, the section has three kinds of tasks. In one, you complete missing letters in short academic paragraphs, which tests whether you recognize words from their context. In another, you read short texts from daily life, such as emails, notices and posts. In the third, you read an academic passage, which is shorter than in the old version of the test. The section is also adaptive: the first module decides how difficult the second one will be.

Across all three tasks, the hardest questions ask for an inference. A notice that says the library will close at nine does not say that students cannot study there at ten, but that must be true. The wrong options are not random. A good distractor repeats words from the text and changes one small thing, so a student who scans for familiar words chooses it with confidence.

The strategy that works is almost the opposite of careful reading. Skim first for the main idea, pace yourself so that the last passage gets the same attention as the first, and eliminate options that could be true but are not supported by the text. And once you have chosen, do not second-guess yourself because of a hunch. Change an answer only when a line in the text proves that you were wrong.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from the publicly described format of the TOEFL iBT reading section as of 2026.

items.situation: A classmate reads every word of the passage before looking at the questions. Give advice in two sentences.
tips: Skim the passage first for the main idea, and then scan for the detail each question needs. Reading every word will make you run out of time.

items.situation: A student finished the reading section in ten minutes. Say what must be true.
tips: He can’t have read the passages carefully, so he must have skipped some questions.
can’t have + participle, must have + participle.

items.situation: Explain what a distractor is, without using the word distractor.
tips: It is a wrong answer that uses the same words as the text, so it looks right.
A relative clause: a wrong answer that looks right.

items.situation: Your friend changed three correct answers at the end. Say what probably happened.
tips: She must have second-guessed herself, or she might have followed a hunch instead of the text.

items.situation: Describe the adaptive design of the reading section in one sentence.
tips: The section is adaptive, so the level of the second module depends on how you did in the first.

items.situation: You see an option that could be true but is not in the text. Say what you do.
tips: I eliminate it, because it might be true in real life, but the text does not support it.
